CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Ballet — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the ballet club habit: five beginner positions in miniature, the hot-soup arms, and a slow song that turns the hallway into a stage.

What is this?

Ballet club is gentle, structured movement — positions, posture and slow controlled motion — where the printed skills are Balance & Grace: steady holds and soft, deliberate moves. Ballet is the club where standing still is a real achievement.

What does it mean?

Ballet trains the body’s quiet muscles — posture, turnout, pointed toes — and the mind’s patience: slow counts feel long at four years old. Learning French step names adds the pleasure of secret vocabulary.

What does the child need to know?

Bare feet or soft shoes, a strip of clear floor, and one slow classical or gentle song. A full-length mirror helps but a window reflection works fine.

Why this matters

Ballet builds posture, balance and body control better than almost any activity — and it teaches practice culture: tiny movements repeated until they look easy. It is also the gateway vocabulary behind figure skating, gymnastics and every movie dance scene.

What it teaches

Balance on one foot, posture muscles, slow-motion control, listening to counts, following multi-part instructions, and performance calm.

Words to learn

first positionpliétiptoearabesquebalancegracebowstage

Say this to your child

“"Ballet club is open! Heels together, toes out — first position. Now carry the hot soup on your arm and walk on tiptoes... no spills! Slow dancers are the strongest dancers."”

Step by step

  1. Warm up: roll the shoulders, point and flex the feet ten times.
  2. First position: heels together, toes out — hold for a slow count of five.
  3. Hot-soup arms: one arm round and forward, walking on tiptoes without spilling.
  4. The slow dance: one gentle song, moving only in slow motion, ending in a held balance.
  5. The ballet bow: one foot behind, a small dip, head up — every class ends with one.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the dancer’s standing leg is straight and strong while the other points back in arabesque — the lift looks effortless because every muscle underneath is working.

Ask your child

"Show me first position." "How do we walk so the soup never spills?" (slow, tiptoes) "Why do dancers practice so slowly?" (control is the skill) "How does class end?" (a bow)

What your child can say or do

Your child may practice positions in the supermarket line, teach the family the hot-soup arms, or demand the slow song twice — ballerinas know their program.

Out in the real world

Ballet training hides inside figure skating, gymnastics, cheerleading and every musical — choreographers borrow its positions the way chefs borrow the knife grip.

Try it together

Swan lake in the hallway: one slow song, arms as wings, one grand walk the length of the hall, one held balance, one bow. Repeat until the audience demands an encore.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are first position’s feet doing?" (heels together, toes out) "What do the arms carry?" (the hot soup) "Name a ballet skill that is slow." (tiptoe walk, arabesque)

This lesson pairs with the Ballet flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.
